sections.title: Cap and form
sections.text: Leccinum versipelle, the orange birch bolete, is a medium to large bolete. At maturity its cap is often 8–20 cm wide, broadly convex, and covered with a finely downy surface ranging from yellow-orange to orange-brown; the margin often slightly overhangs the tubes and may be irregular. Colour varies and is not an absolute diagnostic character; rare pale forms are reported.

sections.title: Tubes, pores and stem
sections.text: The hymenophore consists of mouse-grey to pale tubes ending in small pores that may become ochre with age; there are no gills. The stem is often long and robust, whitish to pale grey or yellowish, and covered with dark-brown to blackish woolly scabers. The pores and tube ends may stain when bruised. The spore print is ochraceous brown.

sections.title: Flesh and habitat
sections.text: The cap flesh is firm and white when cut, then may gradually turn grey and eventually nearly black, sometimes with a violet tinge. In the stem the change can be more pronounced: grey near the top and blue-green to blackish toward the base. The intensity varies between specimens. This is a mycorrhizal fungus usually associated with birch in Europe; regional sources also report it beneath other broadleaf trees. It grows on the ground, mainly in summer and autumn.

sections.title: Distinguishing it from Leccinum scabrum and food safety
sections.text: Both species may occur beneath birch. L. versipelle most often has an orange to orange-brown cap and its flesh stains more strongly after cutting; L. scabrum usually has a grey-brown cap and flesh that changes little. These are tendencies, not guarantees: colour varies, and staining depends on the tissue and specimen. DGfM includes L. versipelle in its positive list of edible mushrooms, while E-Flora BC notes that it may cause gastric distress in some people. Do not eat it based on a photograph alone; have the identification confirmed and cook it thoroughly. Contact a poison centre or emergency services if symptoms follow ingestion.

traits: Often broad cap (8–20 cm), convex, yellow-orange to orange-brown and finely downy; colour is variable
Mouse-grey to pale tubes ending in small pores that may become ochre with age — never gills
Whitish to pale-grey, often robust stem covered with dark-brown to blackish woolly scabers
White flesh when cut, which may turn grey then very dark; the stem base can stain locally blue-green
Mycorrhizal, mainly beneath birch in Europe; summer and autumn; ochraceous-brown spore print
safetyNote: DGfM includes Leccinum versipelle in its positive list of edible mushrooms, but E-Flora BC notes possible gastric distress in some people. Eat it only after reliable identification and thorough cooking; a photograph or this page is not enough to determine that a mushroom is safe to eat. Contact a poison centre or emergency services if symptoms follow ingestion.
